newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo exporters plead for weaker dinar.
newsitem.headline: Yugo exporters plead for weaker dinar.

text.p: A survey of Yugoslav exporters showed they would welcome a lower dinar exchange rate to help them re-enter foreign markets, but economists said on Wednesday any devaluation could bring a surge in prices.
The country's trade gap topped one billion dollars from January to July, with exports standing at $936.5 million and imports at $1.937 billion.
According to a monthly survey by the Institute for Market Research (IZIT), exporters say they could improve their performance with a more supportive dinar exchange rate.
But IZIT economists see the call for weaker dinar unjustified even though the dinar's stability has been accompanied by high inflation.

"From the exporter's point of view the dinar is overvalued. But we think the government should not give in to those calls and devalue the dinar," the institute's Tomislav Milisavljevic told reporters.
Instead he suggested all exporting companies should raise productivity and improve the quality of their products.
Zivojin Jevtic of the Belgrade-based Foreign Trade Research Institute also told Reuters that devaluation would be negative.
"If the government gave up to those pressures, it would face new demands for reintroducing subsidies to agriculture and the economy would re-enter a vicious circle," he said.
Jevtic said that a return to the old socialist system of two or more dinar exchange rates would translate into higher prices for domestic customers.
According to the latest figures provided by IZIT, the average monthly inflation from January to July stood at 5.1 percent, corresponding to an annual 82 percent inflation rate.
In June the central bank vice-governor Zarko Trbojevic told an annual banking conference that the dinar forex rate would remain fixed at 3.3 to the German mark until the end of 1996.
"The government has sufficient reserves to defend the dinar," Trbojevic told bankers, but he admitted the expanding trade deficit posed a huge problem for the economy.
The dinar was last devalued by almost 70 percent to its current level in November 1995 to bring it in line with the prevailing black market rate.

Since then, the gap between the official and the black market rate stood at less than ten percent. The current black market rate is 3.35 per German mark. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
